Saying: Spare the rod, spoil the child
WhatItMeans: Most people who quote it mean that children who are not disciplined firmly will turn out spoiled, and that physical discipline is what the Bible prescribes.
WhatTheBibleSays: Proverbs 13:24 does say, "He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes," and Proverbs 22:15 and Proverbs 23:13-14 speak of correction in the same spirit, while Hebrews 12:6 says the Lord chastens those He loves. But a proverb is wisdom to weigh, not a command to strike, and the Bible's picture of discipline is loving, timely correction, never cruelty. My position is that the rhyme itself is not a verse, while the heart of it — loving discipline that does not leave a child to himself — is genuinely biblical.
Origin: Samuel Butler's satirical poem Hudibras, Part II (1664), where the line appears in a passage about lovers, not children: "Love is a boy by poets styl'd; Then spare the rod, and spoil the child." Butler was riffing on Proverbs 13:24, not quoting it.
Sources: Butler, Hudibras, Part II (1664); on-site KJV text of Proverbs 13:24, Proverbs 22:15, Proverbs 23:13-14 and Hebrews 12:6
